Bush]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Texas sidebar}} The '''1998 Texas gubernatorial election''' was held on November 3, 1998, to elect the [[governor of Texas]]. [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent [[George W. Bush]] was re-elected in a landslide over [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] [[Texas Land Commissioner]] [[Garry Mauro]], with 68 percent of the vote. The landslide victory established Bush as the early front-runner for the [[2000 Republican Party presidential primaries|2000 Republican Party presidential nomination]], which he ultimately won before winning the [[2000 United States presidential election|2000 presidential election]]. Bush carried 239 counties, while Mauro carried just 15. Exit polls revealed that Bush won 27 percent of the African American vote, the highest percentage for any Republican statewide candidate in the country, and 49 percent of the Latino vote. This was the first election in which Republicans won consecutive gubernatorial elections in the state. Bush's 37-point margin of victory was the largest won by any candidate since [[1964 Texas gubernatorial election|1964]] and is, to date, the largest ever won by a Republican candidate. As of {{CURRENTYEAR}}, this is the most recent gubernatorial election in which [[El Paso County, Texas|El Paso]], [[Hidalgo County, Texas|Hidalgo]], [[Willacy County, Texas|Willacy]], or [[Travis County, Texas|Travis]] counties voted for the Republican candidate, with Travis giving Bush over 60 percent of its vote, a rarity for Republicans in that county given its status as a liberal stronghold.{{efn|Despite El Paso going for Bush in this election, they would fail to back him in either of his presidential campaigns in 2000 and 2004. Travis County gave Bush a plurality in 2000 before reverting to Democratic hands in 2004.}} Bush was sworn in for a second term as governor on January 19, 1999. He resigned on December 21, 2000, after his election as the 43rd [[president of the United States]]. Lieutenant governor [[Rick Perry]] served the remainder of Bush's term. ==Background== George W. Bush, the son of former [[President of the United States|United States president]] [[George H. W. Bush]], was elected governor in [[1994 Texas gubernatorial election|1994]] by defeating [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] incumbent [[Ann Richards]]. Upon taking office in January 1995, Bush had a low approval rating of 38 percent. However, his popularity improved significantly over the course of his first term, reaching 70 percent in February 1997.{{cite news|url=http://www.texnews.com/local97/rate111697.html|title=Governor has highest rating in more than a decade|author=Steve Ray|date=November 16, 1997|newspaper=[[Abilene Reporter-News]]|access-date=June 9, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20131220032128/http://www.texnews.com/local97/rate111697.html|archive-date=2013-12-20|url-status=dead}} Going into the election, Bush had an approval rating of 76 percent.{{cite book|author=Beatrice Gormley|title=President George W. Bush|publisher=Aladdin Paperbacks|location=New York|pages=108–109|chapter=Making The Big Run|date=14 December 2000|isbn=0-689-84410-7|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OF6jyYRjaUkC&pg=PA108 |access-date=May 10, 2013}} ==Primaries== ===Republican=== {{Election box begin no change |title = Republican primary results }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change |candidate = [[George W. Bush]], incumbent [[governor of Texas]] since 1995 (Republican) * [[Garry Mauro]], [[Texas General Land Office|Texas land commissioner]] (Democratic) * Susan Lee Solar (Independent) * Lester R. Turlington Jr. (Libertarian) === Campaign === Before the campaign began, George Bush spokeswoman [[Karen Hughes]] said, "The philosophical differences between Gov. Bush and Garry Mauro are clear and stark. Gov. Bush is a conservative, as most Texans are, and Garry Mauro is a liberal."{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=861&dat=19971117&id=9dJHAAAAIBAJ&pg=1158,2728201|title=Mauro Hits Trail To Challenge Bush|date=November 17, 1997|agency=[[Associated Press]]|newspaper=[[The Victoria Advocate]]|page=2|access-date=May 8, 2013|location=Austin, Texas}} On June 22, 1998, Mauro called Bush out of touch saying, "Governor Bush is out of touch with the concerns of ordinary citizens and in bed with the giant HMO's." This was because in 1995, Bush vetoed the Patient Protection Act, which would have forced state-regulated healthcare organizations to allow their customers to choose their own doctor. The Patient Protection Act would have also mandated that insurance companies to cover cancer treatment received at the [[University of Texas MD Anderson Cancer Center]].{{cite news|url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/politics/campaigns/keyraces98/stories/lstx062398.htm|title=Texan Mauro Tries Democrats' Health Care Election Theme in Snipe At Bush|author=Brian Carlson|date=June 23, 1998|newspaper=[[The Washington Post]]|access-date=May 10, 2013 }} Bush and Mauro met for the sole gubernatorial election debate in El Paso on October 16, 1998. Initially, Bush seemed rather nervous and defensive. Mauro attacked Bush for his position on teachers salaries and support for a [[Radioactive waste|nuclear waste dump]] in [[Sierra Blanca, Texas|Sierra Blanca]]. However, Bush was well prepared and attacked Mauro's tax and spending proposals, describing them as "overambitious".{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=LEEKAAAAIBAJ&pg=5257,4470291&dq=bush+vs+mauro+debate&hl=en|title=After the debate|author=Dave McNeely|date=October 22, 1998|newspaper=[[The Victoria Advocate]]|page=5|access-date=May 10, 2013}} The results of the debate would have little impact on the general election in November. === Polling === Throughout the entire campaign, George W. Bush led in the polls by wide margins. After Garry Mauro declared his candidacy in November 1997, a Scripps Howard Texas Poll of 793 registered voters showed Bush leading by 68%–16%, with 14% undecided. In mid-June 1998, a Scripps Howard Texas Poll was conducted with Bush versus Mauro. The poll showed 70% likely voters support Bush, 17% favored Mauro, 11% were undecided, and 2% would vote for neither. Bush's approval rating was also virtually unchanged polling at 75%. In response to the poll, government professor Bruce Buchanan at the [[University of Texas at Austin]] said, "Gov. Bush looks to be unbeatable, but there's enough time for anything to happen. There is a slim chance for Mauro but still a real chance for him to reach voters with ad dollars and issue choices. It's just too early to call the November election in June."{{cite news|url=http://www.texnews.com/1998/texas/texpoll0618.html|title=Poll shows Bush in a clear lead over Mauro in governor's race|author=Anna M. Tinsley|date=June 18, 1998|newspaper=[[Abilene Reporter-News]]|access-date=May 8, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20041026023341/http://www.texnews.com/1998/texas/texpoll0618.html|archive-date=2004-10-26|url-status=dead}} Another Scripps Howard Texas Poll was conducted from August 12 to August 27, 1998. It indicated that 77% of likely voters support Bush, 20% favored Mauro, and 1% supported Libertarian candidate Lester Turlington Jr. About 10% were undecided and 2% didn't answer. Again, Bush's approval rating barely fell and was 74% of Texans remarked that he was doing a good to excellent job as governor. Allan Saxe, an assistant political science professor at the University of Texas said, "Now he's ahead [Bush] by an awfully huge margin. If Garry Mauro can close that to a 10 to 15 percent difference by election day, it will be a symbolic victory. But it will be hard to do – a 50-point difference is a big one." Among Hispanics, Bush led Mauro 51%–31%, down from 67%–20% in June.{{cite news|url=http://texnews.com/1998/local/poll0901.html|title=Poll shows Bush would take easy win over Mauro|author=Anna M. However, Mauro himself never sought political office again. Eventually, he opened a [[Practice of law|private law practice]] in his hometown of Austin.{{cite news|url=http://blog.chron.com/txpotomac/2010/03/where-are-they-now-garry-mauro/|title=Where Are They Now? Garry Mauro|date=March 18, 2010|publisher=[[Houston Chronicle]]|access-date=May 10, 2013}} George W. Bush was inaugurated for his second term as Governor of Texas on January 19, 1999. With his brother [[Jeb Bush|Jeb]] sworn-in as [[Governor of Florida]] earlier that month, George and Jeb Bush became the first two brothers to simultaneously serve as governors since [[Nelson Rockefeller|Nelson]] and [[Winthrop Rockefeller]] from 1967 to 1971. In June 1999, Bush announced his candidacy for president in 2000.{{cite report|url=http://www.georgewbushlibrary.smu.edu/The-President-and-Family/George-W-Bush.aspx|title=The President & Family George W. Bush|publisher=[[George W. Bush Presidential Center]]|access-date=May 10, 2013|location=Dallas, Texas}} At the [[2000 Republican National Convention]], Bush was nominated for president, and he narrowly won the general election against Al Gore. On December 21, 2000, less than two years into his second term, George W. Bush resigned as governor and was succeeded by [[Rick Perry]].{{cite report|url=https://www.tsl.state.tx.us/governors/modern/page3.html|title=Modern Texas Part 3, 1991–present|date=September 20, 2011|publisher=[[Texas State Library and Archives Commission]]|access-date=May 10, 2013|location=Austin, Texas}} ==Notes== {{notelist}} ==References== {{reflist}} ==External links== '''Official campaign websites (archived)''' *[https://web.archive.org/web/19981111185031/http://www.bush98.com/ George W.
